Great Tables turns DataFrames into display tables: the kind of table you'd find in a report, a
journal article or on a web page. Give a table a header and footer, group and label its rows and
columns, format every kind of value, and style any part of it. Then, if you like, hand it to your
readers to sort, filter and search in the browser.

## Build a table, one layer at a time {.gth-heading}

A table is made by chaining methods onto `GT()`, each adding a part of the table, a format or a
style. Step through the layers of this one to see what each adds; the new lines of code are
highlighted.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "How `countries` is made"
#| classes: gth-prep
import polars as pl
from great_tables import GT, GTI, data, loc, md, nanoplot_options, style

regions = {
    "IN": "Asia", "CN": "Asia", "ID": "Asia", "PK": "Asia", "BD": "Asia",
    "US": "Americas", "BR": "Americas",
    "NG": "Africa",
}

# The eight most populous countries of 2022, with their populations in 1960 and 2022, and
# (in millions) every five years between
countries = (
    data.pl.countrypops
    .filter(pl.col("country_code_2").is_in(list(regions)))
    .sort("year")
    .group_by("country_code_2", "country_name", maintain_order=True)
    .agg(
        pop_1960=pl.col("population").first(),
        pop_2022=pl.col("population").last(),
        trend=(pl.col("population") / 1e6).round(1).filter(pl.col("year") % 5 == 0),
    )
    .with_columns(
        region=pl.col("country_code_2").replace_strict(regions),
        change=pl.col("pop_2022") / pl.col("pop_1960") - 1,
    )
    .sort("pop_2022", descending=True)
    .select("country_code_2", "country_name", "region", "pop_1960", "pop_2022", "change", "trend")
)
```

::::: {.gth-stepper}

:::: {.gth-step .gth-step-raw}
[Data]{.gth-step-name}

It starts with a DataFrame: here, the eight most populous countries, from `data.countrypops`.
`GT()` takes Polars, Pandas and PyArrow tables as they are.

```{python}
GT(countries)
```
::::

:::: {.gth-step}
[Structure]{.gth-step-name}

Add a title, group the rows by region, put a spanner over the population columns, label the
columns and cite the source.

```{python}
(
    GT(countries, groupname_col="region")
    .tab_header(
        title="The world's most populous countries",
        subtitle="And how they've grown since 1960",
    )
    .tab_spanner(label="Population", columns=["pop_1960", "pop_2022"])
    .cols_label(
        country_code_2="",
        country_name="Country",
        pop_1960="1960",
        pop_2022="2022",
        change="Change",
        trend="1960–2020",
    )
    .tab_source_note(
        md("Source: [The World Bank](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SP.POP.TOTL).")
    )
)
```
::::

:::: {.gth-step}
[Format]{.gth-step-name}

Turn country codes into flags and populations into millions and billions, show the change as a
percentage, and draw each list of populations as a small plot.

```{python}
(
    GT(countries, groupname_col="region")
    .tab_header(
        title="The world's most populous countries",
        subtitle="And how they've grown since 1960",
    )
    .tab_spanner(label="Population", columns=["pop_1960", "pop_2022"])
    .cols_label(
        country_code_2="",
        country_name="Country",
        pop_1960="1960",
        pop_2022="2022",
        change="Change",
        trend="1960–2020",
    )
    .tab_source_note(
        md("Source: [The World Bank](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SP.POP.TOTL).")
    )
    .fmt_flag(columns="country_code_2")
    .fmt_number(columns=["pop_1960", "pop_2022"], compact=True, decimals=1)
    .fmt_percent(columns="change", decimals=0, force_sign=True)
    .fmt_nanoplot(columns="trend", options=nanoplot_options(show_data_points=False))
)
```
::::

:::: {.gth-step}
[Style]{.gth-step-name}

Color each change by its size, set the countries and regions in bold, add a footnote and set the
header to the left.

```{python}
(
    GT(countries, groupname_col="region")
    .tab_header(
        title="The world's most populous countries",
        subtitle="And how they've grown since 1960",
    )
    .tab_spanner(label="Population", columns=["pop_1960", "pop_2022"])
    .cols_label(
        country_code_2="",
        country_name="Country",
        pop_1960="1960",
        pop_2022="2022",
        change="Change",
        trend="1960–2020",
    )
    .tab_source_note(
        md("Source: [The World Bank](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SP.POP.TOTL).")
    )
    .fmt_flag(columns="country_code_2")
    .fmt_number(columns=["pop_1960", "pop_2022"], compact=True, decimals=1)
    .fmt_percent(columns="change", decimals=0, force_sign=True)
    .fmt_nanoplot(columns="trend", options=nanoplot_options(show_data_points=False))
    .data_color(columns="change", palette=["#FFF0FA", "#F900C3"])
    .tab_style(
        style=style.text(weight="bold"),
        locations=[loc.body(columns="country_name"), loc.row_groups()],
    )
    .tab_footnote(
        "Midyear estimates.",
        locations=loc.spanner_labels(ids=["Population"]),
    )
    .opt_align_table_header(align="left")
)
```
::::

:::: {.gth-step}
[Interact]{.gth-step-name}

Change `GT` to `GTI`, and readers can sort, search and filter the table, with every format and
style kept. Try sorting by a column, or filtering by the change.

```{python}
(
    GTI(countries, groupname_col="region")
    .tab_header(
        title="The world's most populous countries",
        subtitle="And how they've grown since 1960",
    )
    .tab_spanner(label="Population", columns=["pop_1960", "pop_2022"])
    .cols_label(
        country_code_2="",
        country_name="Country",
        pop_1960="1960",
        pop_2022="2022",
        change="Change",
        trend="1960–2020",
    )
    .tab_source_note(
        md("Source: [The World Bank](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SP.POP.TOTL).")
    )
    .fmt_flag(columns="country_code_2")
    .fmt_number(columns=["pop_1960", "pop_2022"], compact=True, decimals=1)
    .fmt_percent(columns="change", decimals=0, force_sign=True)
    .fmt_nanoplot(columns="trend", options=nanoplot_options(show_data_points=False))
    .data_color(columns="change", palette=["#FFF0FA", "#F900C3"])
    .tab_style(
        style=style.text(weight="bold"),
        locations=[loc.body(columns="country_name"), loc.row_groups()],
    )
    .tab_footnote(
        "Midyear estimates.",
        locations=loc.spanner_labels(ids=["Population"]),
    )
    .opt_align_table_header(align="left")
    .i_cols_filter(columns="change")
    .i_cols_controls(columns="country_code_2", sortable=False)
    .i_pagination(False)
    .i_responsive("scroll")
    .i_view(sort="-change")
)
```
::::

## Format every kind of value {.gth-heading}

The `fmt_*()` methods format a table's values as numbers, currencies, percentages, dates and times,
durations, units, chemical formulas, flags, icons, images and more, in any of hundreds of locales.
The values themselves are kept: formatting only changes how they're shown. Where formats leave
off, `sub_*()` methods put text in place of missing, zero, small or large values, and `text_*()`
methods transform the text that formatting made.

::: {.gth-gallery}
```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
import pandas as pd

examples = pd.DataFrame(
    [
        ("Numbers", "fmt_number(compact=True)", 2_418_000_000),
        ("Numbers", "fmt_currency(currency=\"EUR\", locale=\"de\")", 1234.5),
        ("Numbers", "fmt_percent(decimals=1)", 0.4567),
        ("Numbers", "fmt_fraction()", 0.875),
        ("Numbers", "fmt_roman()", 2026),
        ("Numbers", "fmt_bytes()", 1_500_000_000),
        ("Dates and times", "fmt_date(date_style=\"wday_month_day_year\")", "2026-11-21"),
        ("Dates and times", "fmt_datetime(format_str=\"EEEE d MMMM\", locale=\"fr\")", "2026-11-21"),
        ("Dates and times", "fmt_duration(input_units=\"seconds\")", 3725),
        ("Science", "fmt_scientific()", 6.02214076e23),
        ("Science", "fmt_units()", "m s^-2"),
        ("Science", "fmt_chem()", "C6H12O6"),
        ("Symbols", "fmt_flag()", "JP"),
        ("Symbols", "fmt_icon()", "star"),
        ("Symbols", "fmt_tf(tf_style=\"check-mark\")", True),
    ],
    columns=["kind", "method", "shown"],
).assign(value=lambda df: df["shown"].map(repr))

(
    GT(examples[["kind", "method", "value", "shown"]], rowname_col="method", groupname_col="kind")
    .cols_label(value="Value", shown="Shown as")
    .fmt_number(columns="shown", rows=0, compact=True)
    .fmt_currency(columns="shown", rows=1, currency="EUR", locale="de")
    .fmt_percent(columns="shown", rows=2, decimals=1)
    .fmt_fraction(columns="shown", rows=3)
    .fmt_roman(columns="shown", rows=4)
    .fmt_bytes(columns="shown", rows=5)
    .fmt_date(columns="shown", rows=6, date_style="wday_month_day_year")
    .fmt_datetime(columns="shown", rows=7, format_str="EEEE d MMMM", locale="fr")
    .fmt_duration(columns="shown", rows=8, input_units="seconds")
    .fmt_scientific(columns="shown", rows=9)
    .fmt_units(columns="shown", rows=10)
    .fmt_chem(columns="shown", rows=11)
    .fmt_flag(columns="shown", rows=12)
    .fmt_icon(columns="shown", rows=13)
    .fmt_tf(columns="shown", rows=14, tf_style="check-mark")
    .tab_style(
        style=style.text(font="ui-monospace, SFMono-Regular, Menlo, monospace", size="0.85em"),
        locations=[loc.stub(), loc.body(columns="value")],
    )
    .tab_style(style=style.text(weight="bold"), locations=loc.body(columns="shown"))
    .tab_options(data_row_padding="5px", row_group_padding="6px")
)
```
:::

## Let readers explore the data {.gth-heading}

A `GTI` table is a `GT` table that readers work with. Give its columns filters and small plots of
their values, and it becomes a way to look through thousands of rows: all of it in the page, with
no server. Here are the 1,851 films in competition at the Cannes Film Festival from 1946 to 2024.
Pick a view below, or use the table's own controls, and the profiles under the column labels show
what's left.

::: {.gth-tour}

```{=html}
<div class="gth-chips" role="group" aria-label="Views of the table">
  <button type="button" class="gth-chip" data-view='{"filter": {"and": [{"col": "director", "op": "contains", "value": "Ken Loach"}]}, "sort": [{"column": "year", "descending": false}]}'>Ken Loach's films</button>
  <button type="button" class="gth-chip" data-view='{"filter": {"and": [{"col": "year", "op": "gte", "value": 1960}, {"col": "year", "op": "lte", "value": 1969}]}, "sort": [{"column": "minutes", "descending": true}]}'>The 1960s, longest first</button>
  <button type="button" class="gth-chip" data-view='{"filter": {"and": [{"col": "countries", "op": "contains", "value": "JP"}]}, "sort": [{"column": "year", "descending": true}]}'>From Japan, newest first</button>
  <button type="button" class="gth-chip" data-view='{"filter": {"and": [{"col": "minutes", "op": "lte", "value": 90}]}, "sort": [{"column": "minutes", "descending": false}]}'>Under 90 minutes</button>
  <button type="button" class="gth-chip" data-view='{"groupBy": "decade", "sort": [{"column": "minutes", "descending": true}]}'>Longest of each decade</button>
  <button type="button" class="gth-chip gth-chip-reset" data-view="reset"><i class="bi bi-arrow-counterclockwise" aria-hidden="true"></i> Reset</button>
</div>
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
films = (
    data.pl.films
    .with_columns(
        minutes=(
            pl.col("run_time").str.extract(r"(\d+)h").cast(pl.Int64).fill_null(0) * 60
            + pl.col("run_time").str.extract(r"(\d+)m").cast(pl.Int64).fill_null(0)
        ),
        decade=(pl.col("year") // 10 * 10).cast(pl.String) + "s",
        countries=pl.col("countries_of_origin").str.replace_all(",", ", "),
    )
    .select("year", "title", "director", "countries", "minutes", "decade")
)

(
    GTI(films, id="cannes")
    .tab_header(title="Films in competition at Cannes, 1946–2024")
    .cols_label(
        year="Year", title="Film", director="Director", countries="Countries",
        minutes="Length", decade="Decade",
    )
    .fmt_integer(columns="year", use_seps=False)
    .fmt_integer(columns="minutes", pattern="{x} min")
    .i_cols_filter(columns=["director", "countries"], type="text")
    .i_cols_filter(columns=["year", "minutes"])
    .i_cols_profile(columns=["year", "minutes"])
    .i_cols_controls(columns="decade", groupable=True, hideable=True)
    .i_export(["csv", "clipboard", "code"], filename="cannes")
    .i_pagination(page_size=8)
)
```

```{=html}
<div class="gth-livecode" hidden>
  <div class="gth-livecode-bar">
    <span class="gth-livecode-title">The code for the rows you see</span>
    <span class="gth-livecode-langs" role="group" aria-label="Library">
      <button type="button" data-backend="polars" aria-pressed="true">Polars</button>
      <button type="button" data-backend="pandas" aria-pressed="false">Pandas</button>
    </span>
    <button type="button" class="gth-livecode-copy" aria-label="Copy the code"><i class="bi bi-clipboard" aria-hidden="true"></i></button>
  </div>
  <pre class="gth-livecode-code"><code></code></pre>
</div>
```

:::

Every view is a query that readers can edit as text (from the `{ }` button), and that
`i_export("code")` turns into the Polars or Pandas code that gets the same rows from the data.
Tables can start with a view of their own, keep the reader's view in the page's URL, open rows to
show their details, link to each other, and fit narrow screens. In Shiny, Streamlit, Panel,
Solara, marimo and notebooks, Python can read and set what readers do.

## Everything a table needs {.gth-heading}

::: {.gth-cards}

::: {.gth-card}
[<i class="bi bi-layout-text-window-reverse"></i>]{.gth-card-icon}

#### Structure

Headers, footers, a stub of row labels, row groups, column spanners, footnotes and summary rows.

[The parts of a table →](/user-guide/header-footer-stub.qmd)
:::

::: {.gth-card}
[<i class="bi bi-palette"></i>]{.gth-card-icon}

#### Style

Style any cell or part of a table, color cells by their values, and choose from premade themes and
fonts.

[Styling the table →](/user-guide/styling-the-table-body.qmd)
:::

::: {.gth-card}
[<i class="bi bi-graph-up"></i>]{.gth-card-icon}

#### Nanoplots

Small line, bar and box plots in the cells of a table, made from each row's values.

[Nanoplots →](/user-guide/nanoplots.qmd)
:::

::: {.gth-card}
[<i class="bi bi-database"></i>]{.gth-card-icon}

#### Any DataFrame

Polars, Pandas and PyArrow tables, and for `GTI` tables, Polars LazyFrames, DuckDB relations and
Ibis tables too.

[The datasets →](/user-guide/datasets.qmd)
:::

::: {.gth-card}
[<i class="bi bi-window-stack"></i>]{.gth-card-icon}

#### Notebooks and apps

Tables show themselves in Jupyter, Quarto, marimo and VS Code, and in Shiny, Streamlit, Panel and
Solara apps.

[GTI in Python and apps →](/user-guide/gti-in-python-and-apps.qmd)
:::

::: {.gth-card}
[<i class="bi bi-box-arrow-up-right"></i>]{.gth-card-icon}

#### Export

HTML and LaTeX, images and PDFs, and with gridwell, Word, Excel, PowerPoint, RTF, Typst and SVG.

[Exporting and saving →](/user-guide/exporting-and-saving.qmd)
:::

## Get started {.gth-heading}

Install Great Tables from PyPI:

```bash
pip install great_tables
```

Then head over to the [User Guide](/user-guide/introduction.qmd) to make your first table, or look
through the [Examples](/examples/) for ideas.
